chunks: "The two main ones are silicon carbide and gallium nitride, with gallium oxide and diamond as longer-term research. They're called wide-bandgap because the gap is about 3.
3 eV, versus 1. 12 for silicon. A wider gap gives a higher critical breakdown field, around ten times silicon's.

A power device blocks voltage across a drift region, and with a ten-times higher field that region can be much thinner and more heavily doped, so for the same voltage rating you get a much lower on-resistance and much smaller capacitances.
That means lower conduction loss and faster switching, which allows higher frequency and smaller magnetics. SiC is the high-voltage one. 650 volts to 3.
3 kilovolts and beyond, with good thermal conductivity, used in EV inverters and on-board chargers.
GaN is lateral and mostly 15 to 650 volts, with very low gate and output charge, so it goes to megahertz switching, used in chargers and totem-pole PFC. The trade-offs are real.
Cost is higher than silicon. SiC MOSFETs need higher gate drive, around 15 to 20 volts, have a lower threshold and a high-Vf body diode.
GaN HEMTs have a low maximum gate voltage, around 6 volts, no real body diode, no avalanche rating, and dynamic on-resistance effects.
And both switch with very high dv/dt and di/dt, so layout inductance and ringing become the main design problem."
